claims.text: Conventional TOR-TILD EAM references inadequately represent the diverse atomic configurations present in ab initio HEA liquids.
The inadequate EAM representation leads to larger thermodynamic-integration errors or path mismatch.
The proposed reference is a machine-learning interatomic potential trained on ab initio configurations from both liquid and near-melting solid states.
Spectral neighbor analysis potentials or moment tensor potentials are candidate methods for constructing the reference.
The machine-learning potential will provide a detailed representation of local atomic environments, many-body interactions, and dynamic disorder.
Training on a comprehensive ensemble that includes highly disordered liquid configurations will more accurately represent the alloy's complex energy landscape.
A more accurate representation of the energy landscape will improve phase-space overlap between the machine-learning reference and the ab initio target.
Improved reference-target phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to conventional EAM references.
The intervention is predicted to reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 20–30% relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The resulting free energies are predicted to be within a few meV per atom of full ab initio benchmarks.
The proposed applicability range is high-entropy alloys containing five or more principal elements.
The proposed temperature range is approximately within ±5% of the alloy melting temperature.
The intervention is expected to be effective for multicomponent high-entropy alloys near melting.
The benefits may diminish for binary alloys, fully ordered systems, or systems far below their melting temperatures because configurational diversity is less critical there.
The estimated 20–30% improvement is based on analogous successes in elemental and binary systems.
The exact numerical improvement requires calibration against full ab initio free-energy calculations.
Failure to reduce path mismatch by at least 20–30% relative to the EAM control would falsify the hypothesis.
A deviation greater than 5 meV per atom from the full ab initio free-energy benchmark would falsify the hypothesis.
